toc.title: Why would you put your own safety at risk?
Moving on can mean a boundary

blocks.p: This one is about toxicity, behavior, and personal boundaries, to help you prioritize yourself and maybe get a bit more unstuck. These are my general thoughts about general situations. Any particular situation you're in could be very different.
A listener from South Africa wrote in with this:

q: I've done some research with regards to toxic people, but can't seem to wrap my head around how to go about a situation where the individual is "too toxic." I feel it's important to determine whether this individual deserves love beyond the ultimate natural form, where you go beyond basic love and help your friend who has some toxic behavior, possibly at the cost of your own safety. Or whether it's more important to recognize their level of toxicity and slowly disconnect from them to value your own security and self-development.

blocks.p: I'm going to go through this in three basic chunks.

Toxic, toxicity. Along with narcissistic and gaslighting, this is one of those words that has lost its meaning. People have stretched it so far, I don't even know what we're talking about anymore. I kind of get the idea. But definitions are pretty darn important. We have to have accurate definitions to build concepts from, and we can't discuss what "too toxic" is without first discussing what toxic is.

So rather than defining it, I want to neutralize the impact of the word. If we get wrapped up in who's toxic or too toxic, we might lose sight of the behavior and focus instead on judging that person, or giving them a broad, sweeping label. In these situations, I think we have to drill down and define what it is that they are doing. What's the behavior that is not working for us?

Take the judgment and the label out of it. What are they doing, specifically? Is it the whole person? Probably not. Or maybe it is. Is it one aspect, a piece of their personality? What are they specifically doing that has earned them this label from you? It can't just be because you don't like them. It can't just be because you feel angry at them.

Toxic is a judgment. The behavior is closer to fact. When we drill down to the behavior, we're getting more concrete, closer to what they're actually doing and not a judgment of who they are. Maybe they deserve the judgment, but that's not what we're talking about here.

A behavior is something you can create a line for. A judgment, not so much. It's a lot more gray, and then you start asking how much toxicity is too toxic. But with a behavior, you can lay it out: "This is okay in my life, and this is not okay. This I'll tolerate. This I will not tolerate." You can get a lot more crystal clear with behaviors than with the general umbrella term of toxic or narcissistic.

Let's get even more specific. Maybe the behavior is lying. They're doing something to get you to believe something that's not true, so they benefit in a selfish way, at your expense, by giving you inaccurate information. Call it selfish lying, malicious lying, whatever you want, but it's lying. That's the behavior.
Generally, I think we can say that lying is not good, and that lying should not be a part of our lives. Each of us has a right to the truth, as close as we can get it.

Say one person in a marriage has a piece of information the other should know, like whether or not they're going to go sleep around with somebody else. It's not a husband and wife thing, it's a spousal thing: the other person has a right to that information. They have a right to clarity about the relationship they signed on for. Marriage is very much a contract. I hate to take the romanticism out of it, but it really is. Or, to keep it simple, if one person breaks the other's trust as part of a mutual, shared, loving relationship, by going outside the norms of that relationship, the other person has a right to know that. Especially if they ask, "Are you cheating on me?" They have a right to an honest answer, even if it's a difficult answer to give or to receive.

So lying might fit into some toxic kind of behavior. But lying is pretty darn specific. You might go into scenarios of "wouldn't it be okay to lie in this situation, or that one?" We're not going there. The point is that it's a specific behavior.

What behavior are you not willing to have be a part of your life, whether it's a relationship, a friendship, or a work relationship? What can you put up with, and what can't you? I'd recommend trying to make it that crystal clear, that black and white.

She says she's having a hard time wrapping her head around this, and I think with these things, it might be more of a feeling. We feel betrayed. We feel deceived. We feel wronged. Those aren't exactly feelings, but I think you know what I'm talking about.

So maybe it's more of a gut instinct thing. When someone's lying, there are often red flags. Things might pop up inside of you saying, "Hey, something's wrong here," before you even learn the truth. So check your instincts. Maybe it's not something you have to wrap your head around. Maybe it's not that complex. Maybe it's more about feeling what's inside of you, your body telling you something's wrong here.
If you're really struggling with whether this person should be in your life, or how much, ask yourself some tough questions:

ul: If this person was not in my life tomorrow, what would be different? What could life be like?
Do they feel more like a weight or a support?

blocks.p: The image that pops into my mind is being a kid at a chain link fence. Kids always have reasons to go over fences, or at least we used to, before all this screen stuff. There was always something on the other side. Sometimes you could make it over, and sometimes you couldn't, and you needed a boost.

So with the person you're thinking about, the one who might be too toxic, or whose behavior you're realizing you're not okay with: if you were at that fence and needed a boost, would they give you one? Or would they be more likely to pull you back, pull you down, or ignore your need for support?

I don't know the answers to those questions for you, and I can't tell you what to do with the answers. But it's not a bad idea to start asking. You're not going to harm anybody by asking yourself questions. They might help you see the other side of things: "I would have more opportunities. I would have more support outside of this friendship or this relationship. I could be a truer version of myself outside of this."

Whatever you decide about these people in your life, I really want you to decide it from a platform of safety, the ventral vagal safe and social state. From that state, we have more access to critical thinking. We can weigh pros and cons. We can be more hopeful and optimistic about our future. The closer you can get to that state before you ask yourself these tough questions, the better.

Once you find your safety state, get access to it, and build your capacity to stay in it, then when you ask yourself these questions, I think the answer is going to be a lot different. I find that for myself. When I think about difficult things from a safety state and not from a defensive state, I get a much different answer. Story follows state.

blocks.h: Why would you put your own safety at risk?

blocks.p: She goes on: "I feel it's important to determine whether this individual deserves love beyond the ultimate natural form." I don't know what that is, the ultimate natural form, or going beyond basic love. Back to the importance of definitions. But I don't think I need to know.
What I'd ask you, dear listener, is this: why would you ever put your own safety at risk? Not just your physical well-being, but your emotional safety as well.

Sometimes we have to feel unsafe to grow. True, absolutely. But situations where we're compromising our values, or potentially compromising our healthy boundaries, are different. Challenging yourself, feeling some defensive state stuff, and growing from it is one thing. This sounds like sacrificing our values and our healthy boundaries to help somebody else who may not belong in our life. That's different.
Going beyond basic love, to me, brings up codependency. That might be one of those overused words too. But my one-liner, my elevator pitch, for codependency is: if you're not okay, I'm not okay.

We have to be okay, even if other people are not okay. In general, you put yourself first, then others. Safety might be one of those lines. If you're sacrificing your safety, your healthy boundaries, or your values, that might be a line. If somebody's lying to you, and your value is that you're not okay with being lied to, that might be where you start to say, "You know what? This isn't working out for me."

Don't sacrifice your own personal values. A value can be a line in the sand right there: "I expect to be told the truth." That doesn't mean people need to tell you their secrets. But when things pertain to you, you have a right to the truth, in general. When someone lies, that crosses the line.

This isn't about what someone else is allowed to do. People make their own choices, and that's out of your control. This is about what you will allow into your life, what you will put up with, the decisions you make for yourself. When they make their choices, your response is under your control, more or less. Hopefully more and more. As you find more safety and have more access to your safety state, you'll have a greater range of possible responses to people's choices. That will look like more control, over yourself at least, not over the situation.
She finishes: "Or whether it's more important to recognize their level of toxicity and slowly disconnect from them to value your own security and self-development."

I would always value your own security and self-development. If you want to be able to help people, you have to come from your own security and self-development. We can only give others the best we have of ourselves. If we sacrifice that for others, we're not really giving them anything. We're actually enabling them to stay the way they are, and depriving ourselves of opportunities to grow.

Of course, this is very situation dependent. What I would focus on is not someone's level of toxicity, but their behaviors. What are they doing or not doing? What is the true impact on you? Does it cross your values or not? Specific things, not toxicity, whatever that means. Otherwise, you're judging their personality and giving it a rating.

Some behaviors might be zero tolerance. Being cheated on might be a zero tolerance thing. Being attacked physically, in my opinion, should be a zero tolerance thing. If it's actually physically dangerous, and you can leave that relationship or that situation, that should be zero tolerance.
If someone's not adding value to your life, if they're not respecting you for the person you are, it is absolutely okay to move on and put yourself first. I'd highly encourage that.

blocks.h: Moving on can mean a boundary

blocks.p: Moving on doesn't have to mean they're out of your life 100%. Moving on could be: you're still in my life, but here are my healthy boundaries. Here's what I'm okay with and what I'm not. Here's where you're allowed to be in my home, or not. Here's when you can see me, or not. Here's when you're allowed to be around my children, or not.

A lot of people, even as adults, have issues with their parents. Maybe their parents were abusive when they were growing up, and now they don't want their parents around their own kids. So they might need a very clear, very strong, very healthy boundary. Not even a line in the sand, but a wall, between their kids and their kids' grandparents. That is completely okay.

Maybe you don't want to kick them out of your life completely. That's fine. Maybe you allow them in your life under certain conditions. I don't think there's a right or wrong answer. That's up to you, and maybe the spouse you're with.

This doesn't make you a bad person. It doesn't make you selfish to put yourself first. It means you're loving yourself and insisting on your own wellness. That is okay, and in my opinion, it's a very good thing. You're only as good to other people as you are to yourself, as much as you've grown for yourself, and then you bring that to other people. If people are doing things that don't cut it in your life, it's okay to move on, or to create a very healthy boundary.

There might be extreme situations where you can't just drop everything and create a new boundary, or get out of that situation. I'm not talking about extreme situations here. I'm talking very generally.

Narrow it down to specific behaviors, which I think you can. Narrow down what you are okay with and what you are not okay with. That's a big piece of creating healthy boundaries: having clear ideas, clear understandings, of what you're okay with and what you're not.

I don't think there's a 100% right answer. Your life doesn't have to look like my life, or like the next person's. We each have different values about our relationships, our friendships, and our families. You have to take your own inventory, and be honest with yourself about what that looks like.
